claims.claim: An event is any observable occurrence in a system or network; a computer security incident is a violation or imminent threat of violation of computer security policies, acceptable use policies, or standard security practices.
An 'imminent threat of violation' refers to a situation in which the organization has a factual basis for believing a specific incident is about to occur.

NIST SP 800-61 describes the incident response process in phases — preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity — and states that response helps personnel minimize loss or theft of information and disruption of services caused by incidents.

Detection and analysis is often the most challenging part of incident response: incidents are detected through automated capabilities (for example intrusion detection systems, antivirus software, and log analyzers) and through manual means such as problems reported by users; signs of an incident are either precursors (a sign an incident may occur in the future) or indicators (a sign an incident may have occurred or may be occurring now).

Containment is important before an incident overwhelms resources or increases damage; most incidents require containment, and it provides time for developing a tailored remediation strategy. Containment decisions (shut down a system, disconnect it from a network, disable certain functions) are much easier to make if there are predetermined strategies and procedures, and delayed containment is dangerous because an attacker could escalate unauthorized access or compromise other systems.
Following standardized procedures should minimize errors, particularly those that might be caused by stressful incident handling situations.

An incident response plan is a written document, formally approved by the senior leadership team, that helps the organization before, during, and after a confirmed or suspected security incident and clarifies roles and responsibilities.

During an incident, distinct roles matter: an Incident Manager leads the response, manages communication flows, updates stakeholders, and delegates tasks without performing technical duties; a Tech Manager serves as the technical subject matter expert; a Communications Manager interacts with reporters and external stakeholders.

All staff should know how to report suspicious events, and organizations should be gracious when people report false alarms and reward people who come forward, as part of a culture of security; NIST recommends that at least one incident reporting mechanism permit people to report anonymously.

Post-incident reviews (NIST 'lessons learned' meetings, CISA retrospectives) should be held within days of a major incident, should examine what happened, how well the response worked, and what to do differently, and must be blameless: security incidents are rarely the result of one person's action and are almost always the result of a failure of the overall system, so the review examines people, processes, and technologies and updates policies and procedures.

CISA advises that all organizations should have clear, executable cyber incident response plans and strategies to protect their own interests and prevent an incident from growing and causing greater harm, and that organizations should report anomalous cyber activity or incidents; CISA Central is the national 24/7 hub for reporting.
An incident response plan should be reviewed regularly (NIST: at least annually) and rehearsed, for example through tabletop exercises in which a facilitator presents a scenario to the team.

U.S. federal statute (44 U.S.C. § 3552) defines an incident as an occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes, without lawful authority, the integrity, confidentiality, or availability of information or an information system, or that constitutes a violation or imminent threat of violation of law, security policies, security procedures, or acceptable use policies.

positions: NIST SP 800-61r2 defines an incident operationally as a violation or imminent threat of violation of computer security policies, acceptable use policies, or standard security practices.

U.S. federal statute (44 U.S.C. § 3552) frames an incident as an occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes, without lawful authority, the integrity, confidentiality, or availability of information or an information system, or a violation or imminent threat of violation of law or security policies.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson leads with the NIST operational definition used in incident handling guidance (the 'working definition, attributed'), adds the everyday gloss 'a security event that harms or threatens the organization,' and notes that federal statute phrases the same idea differently; no single definition is asserted as universal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How the response lifecycle is named
positions: NIST SP 800-61 describes four phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity.
Many curricula teach the cycle in six steps: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn (a popularization aligned with the SANS PICERL-style naming).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the classic cycle as prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn — one line each — and explicitly maps the six steps onto the four NIST SP 800-61 phases, attributing the underlying framework to NIST.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft was treated as editorial intent only; its boilerplate framing (an unattributed 'security event' definition and generic lifecycle wording) was discarded rather than verified, per the topic-agent brief.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced any unattributed incident definition with the attributed NIST SP 800-61r2 definition, with the everyday gloss kept clearly separate.
Named the six-stage classic cycle and mapped it explicitly onto the four NIST SP 800-61 phases so the naming is not presented as NIST's own.
Added the CISA blameless-retrospective requirement and role definitions (Incident Manager, Tech Manager, Communications Manager) to the human-side and learning-after sections.
